content: Mothers who were confirmed to have Zika virus infection and exhibited symptoms within three days of delivery were studied. Among their infants, two out of three were confirmed to have Zika virus infection. The virus was detected in the breast milk of all three mothers, and in one case, the virus was shown to be capable of replication in cell culture. However, the available data is insufficient to definitively conclude that Zika virus can be transmitted through breastfeeding. The overall quality of evidence regarding suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection in infants or young children who breastfeed from mothers with Zika virus infection is very low. This includes the detection of Zika virus RNA (via RT-PCR) or live virus in the breast milk of acutely ill mothers. Surveys conducted in Yap Island (Micronesia), Nigeria, and French Polynesia confirmed the presence of Zika virus in serum and saliva of men and women, but none of these studies included lactating women. Additionally, no studies have investigated the presence of Zika virus in sweat. The ongoing WHO surveillance of the Zika virus outbreak has not reported any adverse neurological outcomes or severe diseases in infants and young children (aged 0–23 months) with postnatally acquired, vector-borne Zika infection. Recommendation: Infants born to mothers with suspected, probable, or confirmed Zika virus infection, or those residing in or traveling to areas with ongoing Zika virus transmission, should be fed according to standard infant feeding guidelines. This includes initiating breastfeeding within one hour of birth, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, and timely introduction of safe and adequate complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding up to two years of age or beyond. This recommendation is strongly supported, as the benefits of breastfeeding in the context of Zika virus transmission outweigh any potential risks. Mothers with suspected or confirmed Zika virus infection, or those who have traveled to areas of Zika virus transmission, are encouraged to breastfeed. However, some mothers may choose not to. Policymakers are advised to adapt breastfeeding policies in the context of Zika virus transmission to most situations. Rationale: Breastfeeding offers significant benefits for both mothers and children across all income levels. Breastfed children experience lower rates of infectious diseases, improved intelligence, and fewer dental issues. For mothers, breastfeeding reduces the risk of breast cancer, improves birth spacing, and may lower the risk of diabetes and ovarian cancer. Scaling up breastfeeding could prevent an estimated 823,000 child deaths and 20,000 maternal deaths from breast cancer annually. Zika virus RNA has been detected in the breast milk of three mothers with confirmed Zika virus infection, and replicative virus was identified in one case. However, there are no documented cases of Zika virus transmission to infants through breastfeeding. The frequency, kinetics, and viral load of Zika virus in breast milk remain unknown. No long-term complications have been reported in the two documented cases of newborns with confirmed Zika virus infection. In countries with ongoing Zika virus transmission, there is scientific consensus that Zika virus infection can cause Guillain–Barré syndrome, including in children under 15 years of age. However, no adverse neurological outcomes or severe diseases have been reported in infants and young children with postnatally acquired Zika infection. Remarks: Mothers who choose to breastfeed should receive skilled support from healthcare workers to initiate and sustain breastfeeding, regardless of their or their infant’s Zika virus infection status. Families and communities play a central role in supporting optimal infant feeding practices. Properly trained community cadres can provide counseling and practical support for breastfeeding and complementary feeding. Multidisciplinary teams may be necessary for infants with feeding difficulties, particularly those with congenital anomalies like microcephaly. Research Priorities: Further research is needed to understand the risk of Zika virus transmission through breastfeeding, the protective factors in breast milk, and the influence of social and cultural values on infant feeding practices during Zika outbreaks. This research may impact future guidance on infant feeding in areas of Zika virus transmission. Implementation and Equity Considerations: The guideline will be disseminated globally through WHO platforms and networks. Member States are expected to adapt the recommendations to their specific settings. Efforts should be made to prevent stigma or discrimination against mothers who choose to breastfeed in the context of Zika virus transmission. Monitoring and evaluation of guideline implementation should include data disaggregated by socioeconomic variables to identify vulnerable populations. Guideline Development Process: This guideline was developed in response to a public health emergency and followed a rapid advice framework. A WHO steering group oversaw the process, ensuring evidence-based recommendations. The guideline will be reviewed within six months of publication to incorporate any new data.
